Revised 2026-10-12 after the second-analyst review in `reviews/REVIEW.md` and its
follow-up `REVIEWS.md`; the point-by-point response is in
`REVIEWS.md`.

## The ask

Do the IRS data show any patterns in nonprofit locations and finances for
Nashville, alongside recent survey work on the Tennessee nonprofit workforce
(see `docs/`)? Exploratory only, five hours, no committed product.
Requester specifics are in the gitignored `_private.md`.

## Geography

Two units are reported throughout.

- **Davidson County** is Metro Nashville. Nashville has a consolidated
  city-county government, so the county is the city. Six small satellite
  cities inside the county (Goodlettsville, Belle Meade, Berry Hill, Forest
  Hills, Oak Hill, Ridgetop) are included.
- **The metro** is OMB CBSA 34980, Nashville-Davidson--Murfreesboro--Franklin,
  TN: Davidson plus 13 collar counties (Williamson, Rutherford, Sumner,
  Wilson, Maury, Robertson, Dickson, Cheatham, Hickman, Macon, Smith, Cannon,
  Trousdale), 2023 delineation, held fixed across years.

Geography is composed by joining the published `county-fips` and `cbsa`
crosswalks onto the geocoded Unified BMF. Location is the organization's
**current** filing address as carried in the BMF, applied to every year of
its history. Organizations headquartered in Davidson (Second Harvest, United
Way, the community action agencies) serve the region, so any per-resident
figure by county overstates how concentrated services are, and nothing in
these data constrains how far a Davidson organization's services reach.

**Benchmarks.** Nineteen peer metros chosen by the analyst (Memphis,
Knoxville, Austin, Charlotte, Raleigh, Indianapolis, Louisville, Columbus,
Kansas City, Jacksonville, Oklahoma City, Atlanta, Denver, St. Louis,
Cincinnati, Richmond, Birmingham, San Antonio, Phoenix). They are not the
Tennessee Nonprofit Network peer states used in the survey brief. The metro
is compared with whole peer metros. Davidson is compared with one county per
peer metro, the county with the most registered organizations. That is a
convenience, not a definition of the central city: it picks St. Louis County
rather than St. Louis city and Henrico rather than Richmond city. Rankings
"of 20" are rankings among these 20 counties or 20 metros. "Peer metros" means all 19 others
combined, including Memphis and Knoxville; "Rest of Tennessee" means
Tennessee outside the 20 metros; "Rest of US" means everything else. The
four groups partition every filer.

## Data

| Source | What it gives | Years | Currency |
|---|---|---|---|
| Geocoded Unified BMF (vintage 2026_09, sha256 in `_pins.csv`) | Every registered organization: current address and classification, ruling date, first and last vintage observed, latest reported revenue and assets | 1989-2026 | Monthly; current |
| E-file v2.1 Form 990 Part I and Part IX (legacy NODC release, slated for supersession) | Employees, volunteers, revenue, expenses, net assets, compensation lines | TY2012-2023 | Lags two to three years |
| NCCS e-file Phase 0 `government_grants` (v2026.06, sha256 verified) | Form 990 Part VIII line 1e | TY2020-2023 | Lags two to three years |
| CORE merged tier, `990combined` (IRS SOI extracts plus legacy; full 990 and 990-EZ) | Filing presence and form type per EIN and year, for the exit trace and the coverage check | TY2019-2024 | Lags two to three years |
| Census county population estimates (vintages 2019, 2023) | Denominators | 2010-2023 | |
| BLS QCEW annual county files | Private-sector average annual pay per job, Davidson | 2019, 2023 | |

**Main population for the financial and workforce tables:** organizations
with current BMF subsection 501(c)(3) that filed the full Form 990,
excluding hospitals and universities (NTEE v2 subsectors HOS and UNI).
Form 990-PF filers are absent because only return type 990 is read. Two
Nashville filers carry a private-foundation code in the current BMF
(Gibson Foundation, Dr Lynn Hicks Foundation); they are kept and noted.
Rows without a BMF match (about 1% of full-990 returns) are dropped.

**Filing selection.** One filing per EIN and tax year, chosen on Part I by
latest return timestamp with the filing identifier as tie-break; Part IX is
joined on the filing identifier, so both parts always come from the same
return. Uniqueness and identity are asserted at build time.

**Definitions.**

- *Employees* is Part I line 5, a calendar-year headcount with no hours.
  *Volunteers* is Part I line 6, the filer's own estimate.
- *Pay per employee* is Part IX lines 5-10 (officer and key-employee
  compensation, compensation of disqualified persons, other salaries and
  wages, pension contributions, other benefits, payroll taxes) divided by
  employees, kept when between $5,000 and $400,000 nominal. It is total
  people cost per head, not a wage rate; many part-time staff read as low
  pay. Medians are over organizations with a valid value; the valid counts
  are in `output/`.
- *Reported line 1e government grants share* is Part VIII line 1e over
  total revenue. Line 1e is grants only; government payments booked as
  program-service revenue (contracts, Medicaid and other reimbursements, on
  line 2) are not included. No figure here measures total government
  revenue. A blank line 1e is treated as zero (see caveat 8).
- *Expenses exceed revenue* is Part I total expenses greater than total
  revenue in the year, including non-operating items.
- *Net assets in months of expenses* is year-end total net assets divided by
  annual expenses, times twelve. Net assets include restricted funds and
  fixed assets such as buildings, so this is an accounting ratio, not months
  of cash or operating reserve, and is not comparable with the survey
  figures on cash on hand.
- Dollars are CPI-U adjusted to 2023 unless stated.

### Limitations and caveats

1. **Filing lag.** The financial and workforce series end at tax year 2023,
   filed during 2024 and 2025. They describe the sector going into 2024 and
   say nothing after that. The survey work in `docs/` covers late 2024 and
   2025. Only the BMF-based counts (density, formation, attrition,
   foundations, zip codes) are current to 2026; the spending and employee
   rows in finding 1 are TY2023.
2. **TY2023 coverage differs between sources.** Compared with the IRS SOI
   extract (CORE merged tier) for the same organizations, the e-file release
   holds 99% as many full-990 filings for TY2023 in the Nashville metro, but
   the two sets differ: 110 CORE filings (6% of the metro's) are absent from
   the e-file release and 88 e-file filings are absent from CORE. For TY2020
   to TY2022 the mismatch is 1-4%. Neither source is complete for TY2023,
   so every 2019-2023 ranking is shown with its 2019-2022 version; where
   they differ, both are stated. (`output/analysis-round1.txt (pass 12)`)
3. **Full Form 990 only.** The 990-EZ (gross receipts under $200,000 and
   assets under $500,000) has no employee count, no compensation breakdown
   and no line 1e, and the 990-N has no financials. The financial tables
   cover a minority of organizations but most of the money. Pre-2021 years
   cover only organizations that e-filed voluntarily.
4. **Leaving the full-990 panel** can mean closure, merger, falling under
   the 990-EZ threshold, late filing, or absence from the e-file release
   alone. The exit cohort was traced through CORE (full 990 and 990-EZ,
   TY2021-2024) and the BMF; the result is in finding 5 and
   `output/exit_cohort_trace.csv`. Whether the organizations with no return
   closed or merged is still not known.
5. **Current address and classification applied to history.** The BMF
   carries one address, subsection and NTEE code per organization. Movers
   and reclassifications are not recoverable. Ruling date is the date of
   exemption recognition, not founding.
6. **BMF first-observed year steps at vintage years** (none in 2017 or
   2021; 14,461 Tennessee organizations first observed in 1989). It is not
   a formation series. Where formation is discussed, ruling year is used.
7. **BMF asset sums by zip code** come from each organization's latest
   return, are missing for 990-N filers, and are dominated by whichever large
   institutions have a mailing address in the zip. They locate large balance
   sheets, not neighborhood resources or need.
8. **Blank line 1e treated as zero.** Line 1e is blank for 63% of Davidson
   full-990 filers in 2023 and 63% outside the 20 metros. The Phase 0
   extraction leaves the amount empty when the XML element is absent, which
   is how a filer with nothing on the line files, but this has not been
   verified against source filings. Blank shares are similar across the
   comparison groups, but equal blank rates do not establish equal missing
   amounts or the same reporting behavior, so comparisons carry the same
   assumption as levels.
9. **Volunteer counts** are self-reported estimates, blank for about one in
   five Davidson filers, and swing with a few organizations (Second Harvest
   reports 25,000; two organizations account for half of Davidson's
   2019-2023 decline).
10. **QCEW is not on the same basis.** QCEW reports wages per annual-average
    job for an industry in a county; the nonprofit measure is compensation
    including benefits per calendar-year head for an NTEE subsector. The
    two are shown side by side, not equated.

## Findings

### 1. Population moved to the collar counties; nonprofit capacity did not

Davidson's share of the metro's registered nonprofits has fallen from 47% in
2000 to 42% in 2026 as the collar grew, but spending and jobs remain in
Davidson and, to a lesser degree, Williamson.

Registered 501(c)(3) organizations (including private foundations) per
10,000 residents, from the current BMF with activity windows applied:

| County | Pop. 2023 | Pop. growth 2010-23 | Orgs/10k 2010 | Orgs/10k 2023 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Davidson | 712,334 | 13% | 49.4 | 58.2 |
| Williamson | 264,460 | 44% | 56.5 | 62.6 |
| Rutherford | 367,101 | 39% | 24.1 | 29.2 |
| Sumner | 207,994 | 29% | 26.9 | 34.5 |
| Wilson | 163,674 | 43% | 28.6 | 34.6 |
| Maury | 110,760 | 36% | 33.0 | 38.4 |

Full-990 charity spending and jobs per resident, TY2023 (caveats 1, 3, 5):

| County | Charity filers | Expenses per resident | Charity employees per 1,000 | Human services expenses per resident | Human services employees per 1,000 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Davidson | 883 | $6,546 | 67.1 | $1,564 | 21.0 |
| Williamson | 331 | $2,994 | 25.7 | $992 | 9.1 |
| Rutherford | 145 | $1,008 | 17.1 | $272 | 2.6 |
| Wilson | 74 | $840 | 7.6 | $104 | 1.3 |
| Sumner | 115 | $441 | 5.1 | $195 | 2.2 |
| Maury | 57 | $1,070 | 12.5 | $176 | 2.9 |

Rutherford is the metro's second most populous county and has grown 39%
since 2010, yet hosts 37 human-services charities filing a full 990 with
2.6 employees per 1,000 residents, against 21 in Davidson. Williamson is
the exception. Every county's organization density rose between 2010 and
2023, so the collar is catching up in counts, not in capacity. Whether that
is a service gap depends on how far Davidson organizations reach, which
these data cannot show.

### 2. Inside Davidson, recently recognized charities cluster in a few zip codes

Among charities active in 2026, ranked by the number recognized by the IRS
since 2020 (current address; caveats 5 and 7):

| Zip | Area | Charities | Recognized 2020+ | Of which human services | Organizations with assets over $10M |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 37013 | Antioch | 273 | 130 | 40 | 2 |
| 37211 | South Nashville | 282 | 115 | 34 | 8 |
| 37203 | Midtown | 337 | 102 | 30 | 32 |
| 37209 | West Nashville | 244 | 86 | 30 | 10 |
| 37215 | Green Hills | 233 | 81 | 23 | 9 |
| 37207 | North Nashville | 177 | 75 | 32 | 2 |

Antioch and South Nashville lead on recent recognitions; Midtown is third
and holds the most large institutions. So recent formation is not simply
"away from the institutions". What the table does show is that Antioch and
North Nashville have two organizations with assets over $10 million each,
and South Nashville eight, compared with Midtown's 32. Full table in
`output/analysis-round1.txt (pass 8)`.

### 3. Formation, attrition, and foundations (BMF, current)

- Nashville's stock of 501(c)(3)s grew 29% from 2019 to 2026, sixth of 20
  metros (Austin 37%, Atlanta and Raleigh 33%). Attrition is close to
  peers: 21% of organizations active in 2019 were gone by 2026 (peer
  median 20%).
- Among charities recognized since 2020, religion is 16% of Nashville's
  against 13% in peers, arts 8.6% against 7.3%, human services 35% against
  38%.
- Private foundations are growing fastest in the collar. Williamson has 7.3
  per 10,000 residents against Davidson's 5.7, and its count grew 48% since
  2015 against Davidson's 23%. The largest remain in Davidson (Dettwiller
  $251M, Scarlett $249M, Frist $196M, HCA Healthcare $193M, Living Legacy
  $165M).
- Most registered organizations are small: among those with a reported
  revenue figure, 60% in Davidson and 58% to 84% in the collar counties
  report under $50,000; roughly three in ten have no revenue figure at all
  (990-N filers and non-filers).

### 4. Funding: human services charities report less in government grants than elsewhere

Reported line 1e government grants as a share of revenue, 2023, charities
excluding hospitals and universities (caveats 1, 8; not total government
revenue):

| | Reporting any line 1e amount | Line 1e / revenue | Human services: line 1e / revenue |
|---|---|---|---|
| Davidson | 34% | 14.8% | 15.7% (13th of 20 peer counties) |
| Nashville metro | 30% | 12.7% | 13.2% |
| Peer metros combined | 29% | 18.5% | 21.6% |
| Rest of Tennessee | 41% | 19.2% | |
| Rest of US | 33% | 14.8% | 23.8% |

Davidson's overall line 1e share matches the rest of the US. The difference
is in human services, where Davidson's charities report 16 cents of revenue
on line 1e against 22 cents in the peer metros and 24 cents nationally;
among the 20 peer counties Davidson is 13th, in the lower half but not an
outlier (Austin 49%, Richmond 3.5%). The collar pulls the metro figure down:
human services charities in Williamson report 1.4% and in Rutherford 3.1%
(all charities: 3.6% and 4.9%), and the 13 collar counties together report
7.8%. Davidson's share has fallen each year since 2020 (17.0% to 14.8%).

The median Davidson charity draws 77% of revenue from contributions and
grants of all kinds (Rest of US 69%). The largest line 1e amounts are
charter school networks (KIPP, LEAD, Valor, RePublic, STEM Prep, each
reporting 84 to 96% of revenue on line 1e), the Tennessee Performing Arts
Center, the Mid-Cumberland community action and human resource agencies,
and Second Harvest.

### 5. Workforce: more organizations, more spending, no more jobs, higher pay per head

Charities excluding hospitals and universities, real 2023 dollars (caveats
1-4). The 2019-2022 column shows the sensitivity to the incomplete TY2023.

| | Filers 2019-23 | Employees 2019-23 | Employees 2019-22 | Real expenses 2019-23 | Median real pay per head 2019-23 | Same, 2019-22 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Davidson | +16% | -5.9% | -1.0% | +5% | +6.9% (1st of 20 counties) | +3.6% (6th of 20) |
| Nashville metro | +26% | -4.4% | -0.1% | +7% | +9.9% (1st of 20 metros) | +7.2% (1st of 20) |
| Peer metros combined | +20% | +17.9% | +9.1% | -3% | +0.7% | -0.5% |
| Rest of US | +16% | -1.9% | +9.1% | +2% | +0.4% | +0.3% |

Employees in this release are lower in 2023 than in 2019 in both Davidson
and the metro, but through 2022 they were flat. The fall may partly reflect
incomplete TY2023 coverage; how much is not established, so it should be
described as observed in this release, not as an established decline. The metro's pay-per-head rise leads the 20
metros under either endpoint. Davidson's leads the 20 counties through 2023
but is sixth through 2022 (Cincinnati leads at +5.5%), so the county
ranking is not robust. Davidson's median pay per head in 2023 was $46,848,
fifth highest among the 20 counties (Atlanta $54,453, Denver $53,436,
Austin $52,809, Indianapolis $47,636).

Human services pay per head in the metro rose from $36,400 to $41,700
(+14.7%). For context only (caveat 10): BLS private social-assistance pay
per job in Davidson rose from $36,900 to $41,500 in 2023 dollars (+12.5%),
and all private pay rose 6.3%. The two measures are not the same thing and
this does not show that nonprofits kept pace with the private market.

The cross-sectional rise exceeds the within-organization change: among
organizations present in both 2019 and 2023, the metro's median real pay
change was +4.1% (peer metros +3.2%, Rest of US +3.5%). Composition is one
possible explanation. Organizations with staff in 2019
that have no full 990 for 2023 in the e-file release had paid less per head
in 2019 than those that stayed: a median gap of $9,900 in the metro (113
leavers with a valid value against 734 stayers; bootstrap 95% interval
-$15,600 to -$4,800) and $4,600 in Davidson (70 against 429; interval
-$15,700 to +$4,200, not distinguishable from zero).

Tracing the 128 metro leavers through CORE and the BMF
(`analysis-round1.R` (pass 11)) shows what "leaving" meant:

| Where the 128 went | n | Median 2019 pay per head |
|---|---|---|
| Last return TY2022 (late or stopped) | 76 | $33,900 |
| Last return TY2021 | 17 | $27,100 |
| Filed a 990-EZ for TY2023 (fell below the full-990 threshold) | 13 | $18,600 |
| No return since TY2020, dropped from the BMF | 17 | $18,200 |
| No return since TY2020, still registered | 5 | $24,900 |

Correction (2026-10-29). An earlier version of this table said 58 of the
128 had filed a full 990 for TY2023 that was in the SOI extract but not
the e-file release, and called nearly half the exits a coverage artifact.
That was wrong: the SOI extract labels a return by the year its accounting
period ends, so those 58 June-year returns were the TY2022 form, not
TY2023. No leaver is in one release and missing from the other. Most
leavers simply last filed for TY2022; whether they are late or have
stopped cannot be read yet.

Among the 115 with no TY2023 or TY2024 return anywhere, the 102 with a
valid 2019 pay value had a median of about $32,000 against $41,600 for
stayers, a gap of $9,600 (interval -$14,000 to -$3,800). The same
construct in the peer metros gives no gap (2,193 organizations; interval
-$2,000 to +$1,600) and in the rest of the US a gap of about +$500. So
the organizations that stopped filing in Nashville had been paying less
per head, relative to survivors, than their counterparts elsewhere.
Whether they closed, merged, or are simply delinquent is not known; 17
have been dropped from the BMF.

Human services charities present in both years went from 34% to 43% with
expenses exceeding revenue (peer metros 39% to 45%, Rest of US 40% to 44%),
while their median net assets rose from 9.6 to 10.8 months of expenses.
Across all Davidson charities in 2023, 40% had expenses exceeding revenue
and 20% held net assets under three months of expenses, both at the
national level.

### 6. Volunteers: more volunteers per paid employee than the national norm, and a declining reported total

2023, charities excluding hospitals and universities (caveat 9):

| | Reporting a positive volunteer count | Reporting any value (including zero) | Median volunteers, positive reporters with staff | Median volunteers per employee | Human services: volunteers per employee |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Davidson | 66% | 81% | 50 | 4.0 | 5.1 |
| Nashville collar | 55% | 67% | 38 | 5.0 | |
| Peer metros combined | 62% | 75% | 50 | 4.1 | |
| Rest of US | 59% | 73% | 34 | 2.6 | 2.5 |

Davidson's human services charities report twice the volunteers per paid
employee of their national counterparts; among the 20 peer counties
Davidson's 4.0 overall sits in the middle (Charlotte 5.9, St. Louis 2.8).
The reported Davidson total fell from 226,840 in 2019 to 173,719 in 2023
(-23%); Hands On Nashville and the Tennessee Environmental Council account
for 26,000 of the 53,000 decline. Among the 377 organizations with a
positive count in both years, the total fell 22% but the median change was
zero: 46% reported fewer, 37% more. In human services 52% reported fewer,
median -7%. Nationally 43% reported fewer. These are estimates from the
retained returns, not a measured change in distinct volunteers or hours.

## Round 2: sector health profile and the listed organizations (draft for review, 2026-10-30)

This section answers the requester's second ask: a profile of the
Davidson County (Metro Nashville) nonprofit and philanthropic sector, and
a filled spreadsheet for the 141 organizations on the team's Ecosystem
Map. It also carries the changes the senior researcher asked for on round
1. Every table names its filing population, because the registry, the full
Form 990, the Form 990-EZ, the Form 990-PF and the 990-N postcard describe
different sets of organizations. "Tax year" means the IRS form year, the
year the accounting period begins; the SOI extract labels returns by the
year the period ends and has been relabeled throughout (see Corrections).

### Corrections to round 1

Three statements in the round 1 findings are withdrawn or changed.

1. **Exit artifact.** Round 1 said nearly half of the organizations that
   appeared to stop filing a full 990 after 2019 had filed for 2023 and
   were missing from the e-file release. That rested on reading the SOI
   extract's period-end year as the tax year. Relabeled, those returns are
   for 2022. No leaver is in one release and missing from the other. Of
   the 128 metro leavers, 76 last filed for 2022, 17 for 2021, 13 moved to
   the 990-EZ and 22 have filed nothing since 2020. The pay gap between
   genuine leavers and stayers is about $9,600 per head on 102
   organizations (interval -$14,000 to -$3,800), not $17,200 on 42, and the
   peer metros show no gap (finding 5, corrected in place).
2. **Release coverage.** Round 1 said the e-file and SOI releases each miss
   5 to 6 percent of the other's 2023 filings. Relabeled, every SOI filing
   for 2023 is also in the e-file release; the gap is one way, and it is
   the SOI 2024 file being partial for fiscal-year filers.
3. **Hospitals and universities.** They are identified by the NTEE-V2
   subsector code, not by name. Two Davidson universities carry an
   undefined code and were inside the charity totals in round 1; they are
   now excluded by EIN, and the all-charity government grant share for
   2023 is 15.5 percent, not 14.8. The justification for excluding them:
   11 institutions account for $10.7 billion of the $15.0 billion that
   Davidson 501(c)(3) full-990 filers spent in 2023, so including them
   turns every aggregate into a statement about those institutions. The
   coverage table shows both populations.

### Who is actually observed: the registry against returns filed

The registry (IRS Business Master File) lists every organization currently
recognized. Most of them file no return with financial information. For
tax year 2023, counting the full 990 from the e-file release and the 990
and 990-EZ from the SOI extract together:

| Davidson County, on the 2026 registry | Registered | Full 990 | 990-EZ | 990-PF | No return seen |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| All registered organizations | 5,146 | 1,151 (22%) | 382 (7%) | 307 (6%) | 3,306 (64%) |
| 501(c)(3), all | 4,472 | 887 (20%) | 311 (7%) | 304 (7%) | 2,970 (66%) |
| 501(c)(3) public charities | 4,067 | 885 (22%) | 311 (8%) | 2 | 2,869 (71%) |
| Public charities excl. hospitals and universities | 4,046 | 872 (22%) | 311 (8%) | 2 | 2,861 (71%) |
| Human services charities | 1,041 | 247 (24%) | 71 (7%) | 0 | 723 (69%) |

"No return seen" covers 990-N postcard filers (receipts under $50,000),
late filers and organizations that have stopped; the releases do not
separate them. About one Davidson charity in five files a full 990, and
those organizations are the population for every financial and workforce
figure below.

### Age, starts and filing gaps

**Recognitions by year** (registry ruling year, organizations still on the
registry in 2026; recognition, not founding; `output/chart_b_starts.png`).
Davidson recognitions ran at 130 to 200 a year from 2014 to 2021, then
rose to 248 in 2022, 266 in 2023, 324 in 2024 and 347 in 2025. Human
services charities followed the same path (45 a year to 2021, 79 to 95 a
year since). Private foundations peaked at 26 in 2023. The recent rise is
partly real and partly survival: older cohorts have had time to lapse.

**Filing gaps** (`output/chart_c_stopped_filing.png`). The registry does
not record when an organization leaves, so two series are kept separate
and never summed. (1) Stopped filing: of Davidson organizations that filed
a 990 or 990-EZ for a given year, the share with no return of either type
in the following two years ran between 3.5 and 6 percent a year from 2016
to 2022, with 2021 (the year after 2020 returns) at 5.8 percent. This is a
two-year filing gap, not a confirmed closure; some file again later. The
figure for 2023 (12 percent) is provisional because the SOI 2024 file is
partial and is not charted. (2) Left the registry: the first registry
vintage in which an organization present by 2018 is absent. The series
steps with the vintages (236 charities in 2017, 116 in 2021, 83 in 2023)
and reflects revocation lists as much as closures.

### How small most organizations are

Total expenses for tax year 2023, Davidson public charities excluding
hospitals and universities, full 990 and 990-EZ filers together (1,184
organizations; 990-N filers, under $50,000 in receipts, are not in any
row; `output/chart_d_expense_distribution.png`):

| Population (tax year 2023) | Filers | 25th pct | Median | 75th pct | 90th pct | Under $250k | Under $1M |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| All charities, full 990 and 990-EZ | 1,184 | $99k | $332k | $1.27M | $5.6M | 43% | 72% |
| Human services, full 990 and 990-EZ | 319 | $103k | $347k | $1.20M | $5.9M | 42% | 73% |
| All charities, full 990 only | 888 | $266k | $655k | $2.38M | $8.5M | 23% | 61% |
| Human services, full 990 only | 248 | $247k | $509k | $1.85M | $8.0M | 25% | 65% |

Among organizations large enough to file either form, half spend under
$332,000 a year and seven in ten under $1 million. Human services
organizations are no larger than the rest.

### Government grants, 2020 to 2023

Reported government grants (Form 990 Part VIII line 1e) as a share of total
revenue, full-990 public charities excluding hospitals and universities,
dollar-weighted (`output/chart_e_govt_grant_share.png`). Line 1e is grants
only; contracts and reimbursements are on line 2 and cannot be separated.
A blank line is treated as zero; about two thirds of filers report nothing
on it, so the median organization's share is zero in every year.

| Share of revenue on line 1e | 2020 | 2021 | 2022 | 2023 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| All charities, Davidson | 17.7% | 16.9% | 16.4% | 15.5% |
| All charities, peer metros | 18.2% | 16.5% | 17.8% | 18.5% |
| All charities, rest of US | 16.4% | 16.5% | 16.4% | 14.8% |
| Human services, Davidson | 17.9% | 14.5% | 14.2% | 15.7% |
| Human services, peer metros | 28.0% | 20.3% | 21.1% | 21.6% |
| Human services, rest of US | 26.2% | 26.0% | 26.5% | 23.8% |

Davidson's human services charities reported a smaller share in every
year, and the gap to the peer metros opened in 2020 and has not closed.
The 2020 peak is visible everywhere; the 990 cannot say how much of it
was federal pandemic relief.

### Filers, spending and employees, 2019 to 2023

Full-990 public charities excluding hospitals and universities, e-file
release (`output/chart_f_filers_spending_employees.png`). Employee counts
on the 990 are noisy and are shown two ways.

| Davidson County | 2019 | 2023 | Change | Same organizations in both years | Change |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Filers | 757 | 881 | +16% | 625 | |
| Spending, 2023 dollars | $4.15bn | $4.39bn | +6% | | +9% |
| Reported employees | 47,861 | 44,948 | -6% | | -0.6% |

Among the 625 organizations present in both years, employees were flat
and real spending rose 9 percent; the 6 percent decline in the full
population comes from the organizations that left or joined it. Through
2022 the same comparison gives -2.8 percent and +4.5 percent. The round 1
claim that part of the employee decline was a release artifact is
withdrawn (Corrections, 1).

### The listed organizations

The team's list names 141 organizations with addresses and no
identifiers. Each was matched by hand to the registry (131 matched; the
10 unmatched are companies, church-run bodies, a Salvation Army unit
under the national exemption, a mutual aid collective, and two
intermediaries with no registry record under their names). The
spreadsheet returned to the team carries, for each matched organization,
tax year 2023 total expenses from the return it filed, with the form and
line named: 92 from the full 990 (line 18), 6 from the 990-EZ (line 17)
and 8 from the 990-PF (line 26, total expenses and disbursements, with
operating expenses and grants paid beside it). Eleven organizations show
only a 2022 full 990 so far; their 2022 figure is given in the status
column. Three matches are flagged low confidence and are with the team.

Against all Davidson public charities, the listed organizations are
older, larger, more often staffed, and more often government funded. The
list was assembled as the organizations active in the team's field of
work, so this describes the list, not the sector.

| Measure | Listed, registered in Davidson | All Davidson public charities excl. hospitals and universities |
|---|---|---|
| Organizations on the registry | 105 | 4,046 |
| Median age (years since recognition) | 23 | 11 |
| Recognized 2020 or later | 12% | 36% |
| Full-990 filers, tax year 2023 | 81 | 872 |
| Median total expenses (full 990) | $1.78M | $627k |
| Median reported employees (full 990) | 20 | 4 |
| Reporting any line 1e grants (full 990) | 60% | 35% |
| Line 1e share of revenue, dollar-weighted (full 990) | 17.0% | 15.6% |

### Who funded whom, 2019 to 2023

Source: grants reported by funders whose registry address is in Davidson
County, on their own returns: Schedule I of the full 990 (recipients over
$5,000 in aggregate, with the recipient EIN) and the 990-PF grants paid
schedule (recipient name and city only, matched by cleaned name and
hand-checked). Recipients are the 116 listed organizations registered in
Davidson; the 15 registered elsewhere are out of scope. Grants to
individuals are excluded. Funders based outside Davidson are absent by
construction, so an organization with no matched grant is not unfunded.

| Tax year | Grant rows | Funders | Listed recipients reached | Total ($M) | of which Schedule I cash | Schedule I noncash | 990-PF |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2019 | 1,379 | 120 | 82 | 30.9 | 19.3 | 0.7 | 11.0 |
| 2020 | 2,116 | 159 | 89 | 56.1 | 34.6 | 2.8 | 18.7 |
| 2021 | 1,041 | 159 | 89 | 43.7 | 23.0 | 1.7 | 18.8 |
| 2022 | 978 | 154 | 88 | 52.7 | 32.2 | 1.4 | 18.9 |
| 2023 | 951 | 154 | 101 | 58.6 | 32.3 | 4.8 | 21.5 |

Over the five years, 104 of the 116 listed organizations received at least
one matched grant from one of 234 Davidson-based funders. The median
listed recipient had 10 distinct Davidson funders; 47 had more than ten
and 11 had one. Funding is concentrated: the largest funder supplied 25
percent of matched dollars, the top three 47 percent and the top ten 70
percent. Twenty-one of the funders are themselves on the list (the
community foundation, the United Way and several foundations), and
grants between listed organizations ran from $20 million in 2019 to
$38 million in 2023; where a listed intermediary regrants, the same
dollar can appear twice.

On "duplication" and "gaps": a shared funder is a shared funder, not
duplication, and no matched grant is not a gap, because the table sees
only Davidson-based funders, only itemized Schedule I recipients, and
only names the match caught. The 2020 Schedule I spike is the community
foundation's itemized COVID-19 relief grants.

### Questions for the reviewer

1. Exits: the two-series treatment above (filing gap through 2022 as the
   primary series, registry vintages as the check), with 2023 withheld.
   Is the two-year rule acceptable, and should the filing-gap chart carry
   the registry series beside it?
2. Comparator for the list: all Davidson public charities as the
   headline, with full-990 filers of similar size as a second column if
   wanted. The list is older and larger on every measure; is the second
   comparison worth the space?
3. 990-EZ filers: included in the expense distribution and in the
   spreadsheet with the form named; excluded from employees and line 1e,
   which the EZ does not carry. Agreed?

## What this could become

- A county capacity map for Metro and the Community Foundation (finding 1,
  with the service-area caveat explicit; the density layer is current, the
  spending layer is TY2023), and a zip-level view of recent recognitions
  (finding 2).
- A funding-mix note on human services (finding 4), new relative to the
  survey work, with line 1e named for what it is. The TY2024 Phase 0 file
  (partial, early filers) could extend it by a year; no TY2024 result exists
  yet.
- The pay and exit pattern (finding 5) now rests on 42 organizations with
  no return since TY2022 or earlier. Before it is cited, those 42 should be
  looked at by name (closure, merger, delinquency) in `output/exit_cohort_trace.csv`.

## Reproducibility

`run-all.R` rebuilds everything: `build.R` (section build-panel) (BMF universe and the
national panel, with the 24 raw e-file CSVs verified byte-for-byte against
their recorded sha256), `build.R` (section build-external) (Census, QCEW and Phase 0
downloads with sha256 checks), `build.R` (section build-peers), then `analysis-round1.R` (pass 1) through
`analysis-round1.R` (pass 12), then `validate-build.R`, which re-derives the filing selection
from the raw Part I files and asserts it matches the panel exactly. Console
output goes to `output/`. Every read is pinned in `_pins.csv` with a
vintage and, for files, a sha256; every BMF read carries the master's
manifest vintage and sha256, and nothing is served from a cache. The BMF is read from a rolling
URL; its manifest vintage and sha256 are recorded so the build can be
identified but not re-fetched once the master rolls. The e-file CSVs
(about 6 GB, 24 files) are those synced for
`requests/2026-06-milwaukee-msa`, identified by sha256 in that folder's
`_efile_inputs.csv`. The folder is therefore reproducible from its inputs
as identified, not from the folder alone.
